overview.what: A can-sized satellite with an ESP32, a pressure sensor and a motion sensor that sends live readings by radio to a second ESP32 and a laptop graph.
overview.why: You learn I2C sensors, radio links and live plotting. You also meet real design limits, such as size, weight and power.
overview.spaceRelevance: Every satellite is sensors, a computer, a radio and power in a small box. CanSats are how students all over the world practise that on a small scale.
overview.finalOutput: A working CanSat, a ground station, a live graph on your laptop and a written test report.
overview.estimatedTime: 4 to 5 weeks at 3 to 4 hours a week

keyIdeas.meaning: Measurements sent from a distant machine to people on the ground. Satellites and rovers send telemetry all the time.
A two-wire bus. Many sensors share the same data and clock wires, and each one answers only to its own address.
Height worked out from air pressure. Pressure falls steadily as you climb, so a pressure sensor works as an altimeter.
A small, fixed-size bundle of bytes sent in one go. Both ends agree on what each byte means.

roadmap.title: What is a CanSat?
roadmap.learn: What a CanSat is, and how it differs from a CubeSat.
roadmap.explain: A CanSat is a model satellite built to fit inside a soda can. Students pack the parts of a real satellite into it: power, sensors, a computer and a radio. It sends its readings to a ground station, where a team watches them. A CubeSat, like the one in the photo, is a real satellite built from 10 cm units. A CanSat is much smaller and is launched only a few hundred metres high, if it is launched at all.
roadmap.implement: Watch the ESA CanSat video. List the four parts every satellite needs, and say which part of your CanSat does each job.
roadmap.outcome: You can explain what a CanSat is and what it needs.

figure.alt: A small box-shaped satellite on a white background with a large gold umbrella-like radar dish opened on top and flat solar panels folded out along the bottom.
figure.caption: RainCube, a real NASA CubeSat with a folding antenna. Its box holds the same kinds of parts as your CanSat: computer, sensors, radio and power.

roadmap.title: Plan the mission and the can
roadmap.learn: What the CanSat should measure, and the size rules that shape it.
roadmap.explain: Real CanSat teams follow ESA's rule: a CanSat fits in 66 mm by 115 mm and weighs 300 to 350 grams. You do not have to compete, but the limits are a good design brief. A good mission is simple and measurable: record temperature, air pressure, height and shaking, and send them live. Height comes from pressure, because air gets thinner the higher you go. Plan how the parts stack before you build.
roadmap.implement: Write a one-line mission, such as: Send temperature, height and motion to a laptop every half second. Draw your own stack inside a 66 by 115 mm outline. Weigh each part.
roadmap.outcome: A written mission and a sketch of the layout.

figure.alt: A soda-can-sized shape 66 millimetres wide and 115 millimetres tall, with a sensor board, an ESP32 and a battery stacked inside, an antenna out of the top, and a note of 300 to 350 grams.
figure.caption: The ESA size limits drawn as a design brief. Ours will be a shape to work to, not a competition entry.

roadmap.title: Wire the sensors
roadmap.learn: How two sensors can share the same two wires.
roadmap.explain: Both sensors talk over I2C, a bus that needs just two wires, called SDA for data and SCL for the clock, plus power and ground. Each device has its own address, like a house number, so many can share the bus. The BMP280 is usually 0x76 and the MPU6050 is 0x68. Both modules run on 3.3 V. The ESP32's default I2C pins are GPIO 21 (SDA) and GPIO 22 (SCL).
roadmap.implement: Wire the ESP32 to the two modules as shown. Check every connection twice before you power up. If the BMP280 is not found later, try address 0x77.
roadmap.outcome: Both sensors are wired to the ESP32.

figure.alt: Wiring diagram: ESP32 3V3, GND, GPIO 22 as SCL and GPIO 21 as SDA each connect to the matching pin on both the BMP280 and the MPU6050.
figure.caption: One bus, two sensors. Power goes to 3.3 V only. Many modules have more pins, but these four are all you need.

roadmap.title: Why pressure gives height
roadmap.learn: How a barometer works as an altimeter.
roadmap.explain: Air has weight. At sea level, a column of air above you presses with about 1013 hPa. Climb, and there is less air above, so the pressure drops. Near the ground it falls about 1.2 hPa for every 10 metres. A barometric sensor such as the BMP280 measures pressure very finely, and the library turns it into height. Weather moves the pressure too, so the sensor gives height above where it started, not above sea level.
roadmap.implement: Watch the video. Then think of a test that is safe: where could you change height by 10 to 20 metres and see the pressure drop?
roadmap.outcome: You know why the pressure falls with height and how to turn it into metres.

figure.title: 17 | Measure altitude with the BMP280 barometric sensor
figure.caption: How a BMP280 estimates altitude and what its readings look like.

roadmap.title: Read both sensors
roadmap.learn: How to read the pressure, temperature and motion in one program.
roadmap.explain: Each sensor has a library from Adafruit that handles the details. Install Adafruit BMP280 Library and Adafruit MPU6050, plus the Adafruit Unified Sensor library they need. At rest, the accelerometer reads about 9.8 m/s2, which is gravity. In free fall it reads close to zero, so you can see when your CanSat is falling. The program notes the pressure on the ground at start, so height reads 0 there.
roadmap.implement: Upload this sketch, open the Serial Monitor at 115200 and watch. Lift the board up and down, and tip it. Take it up a flight of stairs and see the height change.
roadmap.outcome: The Serial Monitor shows temperature, pressure, height and motion.

figure.caption: Reads both sensors every half second. readAltitude() takes the ground pressure in hPa, so it reports height above the start.

roadmap.title: Choose a radio link
roadmap.learn: How data gets from the can to the ground.
roadmap.explain: A telemetry link is the radio path that carries measurements from a spacecraft to the ground. The ESP32 has a built-in way to do this called ESP-NOW. It sends small packets of up to 250 bytes straight between boards, with no router or internet. Ours holds 20 bytes. Reported range is a couple of hundred metres in open air, and far less through walls. A second ESP32 is the ground station: it receives packets and hands them to your laptop by USB.
roadmap.implement: Draw your own copy of the link picture. Label what each box does and what travels between them.
roadmap.outcome: You can trace one reading from a sensor to a laptop screen.

figure.alt: A CanSat ESP32 sends radio packets to a ground station ESP32, which passes them by USB to a laptop. Below is a 20-byte packet made of five 4-byte fields, and a sample line of text.
figure.caption: The packet is a few numbers in a fixed order. Both boards agree on the order, so no labels need to travel.

roadmap.title: Send packets from the CanSat
roadmap.learn: How to pack readings and send them by radio.
roadmap.explain: A struct holds your five numbers in a fixed order. esp_now_send copies its bytes into one radio packet. Sending to the broadcast address FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF means any ESP32 listening on the same Wi-Fi channel can receive it, so there is no address to look up. Both boards must be in station mode, which the WiFi.mode call sets. Keep the antenna end of each ESP32 away from metal and your hands.
roadmap.implement: Add the radio code to your sensor sketch. Upload it to the CanSat board and power it from a USB power bank. It will not print anything useful yet. The next step reads it.
roadmap.outcome: The CanSat sends a packet twice a second.

figure.caption: The new parts only. Keep your sensor code in the places the comments show.

roadmap.title: Build the ground station
roadmap.learn: How a second ESP32 receives the packets.
roadmap.explain: The ground station is a second ESP32, plugged into your laptop. It registers a function that runs each time a packet arrives. That function checks the size, copies the bytes back into the same struct and prints one line of comma-separated text. This sketch uses the callback form from Arduino-ESP32 core 3.0 and newer. If your boards package is older, update it in the Boards Manager.
roadmap.implement: Upload this to the second board, open the Serial Monitor and power the CanSat from the power bank. You should see a new line every half second.
roadmap.outcome: Packets from the CanSat appear on your laptop.

figure.caption: The ground station. It does nothing except pass each packet on as a line of text.

roadmap.title: Draw live graphs
roadmap.learn: How to plot the stream on your laptop.
roadmap.explain: Python can read the lines through the USB port with pyserial and draw them with matplotlib. The loop reads one line, splits it at the commas, turns the pieces into numbers and adds them to a list of the last 120 packets. Then it redraws the graphs. A try and except skips any half-received line. Find your port name in the Arduino IDE, such as COM5 on Windows.
roadmap.implement: Install with pip install pyserial matplotlib. Close the Serial Monitor first, because only one program can use the port. For a first test, swap in made-up lines for port.readline().
roadmap.outcome: A live graph of height and motion follows the CanSat.

figure.code:
import collections
import serial                                    # pip install pyserial
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

port = serial.Serial("COM5", 115200, timeout=1)  # your port, shown in the Arduino IDE
rows = collections.deque(maxlen=120)             # keep the last 120 packets

plt.ion()
fig, (top, bottom) = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)
while plt.fignum_exists(fig.number):
    parts = port.readline().decode(errors="ignore").strip().split(",")
    try:
        rows.append([float(x) for x in parts])   # ms, temp, pressure, height, accel
    except ValueError:
        continue                                 # skip half-received lines
    secs = [r[0] / 1000 for r in rows]
    top.clear();    top.plot(secs, [r[3] for r in rows]);    top.set_ylabel("height (m)")
    bottom.clear(); bottom.plot(secs, [r[4] for r in rows]); bottom.set_ylabel("accel (m/s2)")
    plt.pause(0.05)
figure.caption: The live view. The first column is milliseconds, then temperature, pressure, height and total acceleration.

roadmap.title: Power it safely
roadmap.learn: How to run a CanSat from a battery without risk.
roadmap.explain: The safest way to power it is a small USB power bank, which has protection built in. If you want something smaller, a single lithium polymer (LiPo) cell needs care. Never puncture, crush, short or overcharge one. Use a cell with a protection board and a proper charger. Charge it only where you can watch it, on a hard, non-flammable surface. Retire any cell that swells. Never connect a LiPo straight to the 3V3 pin.
roadmap.implement: Start with a power bank. Watch the LiPo safety video before you ever touch a LiPo, and ask your supervisor first. Tape or cap every exposed wire end.
roadmap.outcome: The CanSat runs from a safe battery.

figure.title: How to keep LiPos from burning down your house (safe lipo charging)
figure.caption: Long, but worth it. It shows what goes wrong with LiPo cells and how to avoid it.

roadmap.title: Pack it and test it
roadmap.learn: How to fit everything in a can-sized shell and test it safely.
roadmap.explain: Stack the parts to match your sketch and hold them with zip ties or foam. Keep the ESP32 antenna clear of metal. Test in order. First walk upstairs with it and watch the height graph. Then test the range in a corridor or field. Only then, with a supervisor, try a drop from low height onto soft ground with a small bag parachute. Never launch it from a roof, drone, balloon or rocket without expert approval.
roadmap.implement: Do the stairs test and range test, and save screenshots of the graphs. If your supervisor agrees, do a drop test from no more than 2 or 3 metres, with the area clear and nobody below.
roadmap.outcome: A tested CanSat and graphs from real tests.

roadmap.title: Publish your CanSat
roadmap.learn: How to document a hardware mission.
roadmap.explain: Space teams write up what they learn. Your report should have the mission, the wiring picture, the code, a photo, your graphs and an honest list of what failed or surprised you. A reader should be able to tell what you measured, how far the radio reached and what you would change on a second build. Include the weight too.
roadmap.implement: Push the code for both boards, the Python graph script, a README with photos and screenshots, and your test notes to GitHub.
roadmap.outcome: Your mission is documented on GitHub.
